lessons.title: Draw resolution-independent graphics with inline SVG
lessons.summary: Embed vector graphics directly in HTML with the svg element: master the viewBox coordinate system, the basic shapes, fill and stroke, text, and accessible titles.
lessons.goal: Build an accessible status badge as inline SVG using viewBox, rect, circle, text and a title element.
lessons.whyItMatters: Icons, logos, charts and badges make up a huge share of the graphics on modern sites, and almost all of them ship as SVG because a vector stays razor-sharp at any zoom level and any screen density. Inline SVG goes further: because the shapes become real DOM nodes, you can style them with CSS, script them with JavaScript, and describe them to screen readers. Knowing when to inline SVG and when to load it as an image is a decision professional front-end developers make weekly.
steps: Read the first two sections to understand what vectors are and how the viewBox coordinate system works.
Study the basic shapes section — rect, circle, ellipse, line, polyline, polygon — and the short path overview.
In the editor, add the svg element with a viewBox of 0 0 200 100 (task 1).
Give the badge an accessible title element as the first child (task 2).
Draw the background rect with a fill and the status circle (tasks 3 and 4).
Add the text label and press Run until every check in the console passes.
lessons.prompt:
<svg viewBox="0 0 200 100" width="200" height="100" role="img">
  <title>Build passing badge</title>
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="200" height="100" rx="12" fill="#e8f5e9"></rect>
  <circle cx="40" cy="50" r="18" fill="#2e7d32"></circle>
  <text x="75" y="58" font-size="20">Passing</text>
</svg>
lessons.explanation: The viewBox declares an internal coordinate space of 200 by 100 units, and the width and height map that space onto the page; scale the element to any size and everything inside stays proportionally crisp. The rect paints the rounded background, the circle draws the status dot, and the text element places a real, selectable label at the coordinates you give it. The title element is invisible but is read aloud by screen readers, which — together with role="img" — turns a silent drawing into an accessible one.
lessons.example:
A team dashboard shows a build-status badge. As a 40-pixel PNG it turns to mush on a retina display and needs a second asset for dark mode.

Rebuilt as inline SVG, the same badge is one block of markup: it renders pixel-perfect at every zoom level, its fill colors can be swapped by a CSS class when the theme changes, and a screen reader announces 'Build passing badge' instead of skipping an unlabeled image.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, complete the status badge: add an svg element with the correct viewBox, give it a title for assistive technology, draw a filled background rect and a status circle, and finish with a text label.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a rounded light-green badge with a dark-green dot and the word 'Passing' next to it, and all five checks pass.
commonMistakes: Confusing viewBox with width/height. The viewBox defines the internal drawing coordinates; width and height define the rendered size on the page. They are independent.
Writing viewbox in lowercase inside an .svg file. In an SVG document the attribute is case-sensitive and must be viewBox; the HTML parser forgives you inline, standalone SVG files do not.
Forgetting that circle uses cx, cy and r while rect uses x, y, width and height — mixing the two attribute sets silently draws nothing.
Shipping an svg with no title or aria-label. Screen readers either skip it or read out raw geometry; decorative graphics should instead get aria-hidden="true".
lessons.proTip: Keep viewBox numbers small and round (0 0 24 24 is the de-facto icon standard). You scale with CSS or width/height anyway, and tidy internal coordinates make hand-editing coordinates painless.

sections.heading: Vectors vs pixels: what SVG is
sections.body:
A raster image (PNG, JPEG, WebP) is a fixed grid of colored pixels. Scale it up and the browser has to invent pixels, so edges blur. SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics — stores instructions instead: 'a circle of radius 18 centered here, filled green'. The browser re-executes those instructions at whatever size is needed, so an SVG is perfectly sharp at 16 pixels, at 1600 pixels, and on a high-density phone screen, all from one file.

SVG is an XML vocabulary, but modern HTML lets you drop an <svg> element straight into the page. Everything between <svg> and </svg> becomes part of the DOM, which is what makes inline SVG so powerful: the shapes can be targeted with CSS selectors, animated, and wired to click handlers exactly like divs and spans.

SVG beats raster whenever the graphic is made of shapes, lines or text: icons, logos, charts, diagrams, badges, illustrations. Raster wins for photographs and anything with continuous, camera-like detail — describing a photo as thousands of vector shapes would be far larger than a JPEG.
sections.code:
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="120" height="120">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="tomato"></circle>
</svg>

sections.heading: The viewBox coordinate system
sections.body:
Every svg element carries its own private coordinate space, declared by the viewBox attribute: four numbers meaning min-x, min-y, width and height. viewBox="0 0 200 100" says 'inside this element, x runs from 0 to 200 and y from 0 to 100'. The origin sits in the top-left corner and y grows downward — the same convention as the rest of CSS layout.

The element's width and height attributes (or CSS sizing) then decide how big that internal space appears on the page. If the rendered box is 400 by 200 pixels, every internal unit maps to two pixels; shrink the box and the drawing shrinks with it. This separation is the whole trick behind 'scalable': you design once in convenient units and let the browser do the mapping.

Two details matter in practice. First, capitalization: viewBox has a capital B. The forgiving HTML parser fixes the casing for you when the svg is inline, but in a standalone .svg file the lowercase form is simply ignored and your graphic may render at a wrong size or not at all. Second, if the aspect ratio of the viewBox and the rendered box differ, the preserveAspectRatio attribute controls the fit — the default letterboxes the drawing rather than stretching it.
sections.code:
<!-- same drawing, three sizes, one set of coordinates -->
<svg viewBox="0 0 200 100" width="100" height="50">...</svg>
<svg viewBox="0 0 200 100" width="200" height="100">...</svg>
<svg viewBox="0 0 200 100" width="600" height="300">...</svg>

sections.heading: The basic shapes
sections.body:
Six shape elements cover most everyday drawing. rect takes x, y, width and height, plus optional rx/ry for rounded corners. circle takes a center (cx, cy) and a radius r. ellipse is a circle with two radii, rx and ry. line draws a straight segment from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2) — note that a line has no interior, so it is invisible until you give it a stroke.

polyline and polygon both take a points attribute: a list of x,y pairs. polyline connects them and stops; polygon automatically closes the shape by joining the last point back to the first, which also gives it a fillable interior. Use polyline for open traces like a sparkline, polygon for closed figures like a triangle or a star.

All shapes are drawn in document order: whatever comes later in the markup paints on top of what came earlier. There is no z-index inside SVG — stacking is purely source order, so put backgrounds first and labels last.
sections.code:
<svg viewBox="0 0 300 120">
  <rect x="10" y="10" width="60" height="40" rx="8" fill="steelblue"></rect>
  <circle cx="120" cy="30" r="20" fill="seagreen"></circle>
  <ellipse cx="200" cy="30" rx="30" ry="15" fill="goldenrod"></ellipse>
  <line x1="10" y1="80" x2="90" y2="110" stroke="black"></line>
  <polyline points="110,110 130,80 150,100 170,70" fill="none" stroke="black"></polyline>
  <polygon points="220,110 245,70 270,110" fill="indianred"></polygon>
</svg>

sections.heading: path, briefly
sections.body:
The path element is the general-purpose shape: its d attribute is a compact command language. M x y moves the pen, L x y draws a line, C draws a cubic curve, A an elliptical arc, and Z closes the shape. Every other shape element could be rewritten as a path — icon sets and vector editors export almost everything as paths.

You rarely write long d strings by hand; tools like Figma, Illustrator or Inkscape generate them. What you should be able to do is read one well enough to spot the moves and lines, and to recognize that a path with fill but no Z may still auto-close for filling purposes while its stroke stays open.
sections.code:
<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100">
  <!-- a simple check mark -->
  <path d="M 20 55 L 42 75 L 80 30" fill="none" stroke="green" stroke-width="8"></path>
</svg>

sections.heading: fill, stroke, and text
sections.body:
Two presentation attributes do most of the styling. fill paints a shape's interior and defaults to black — which is why an unstyled circle appears as a solid black disc. stroke paints the outline and defaults to none, so outlines are invisible until you ask for them; stroke-width sets their thickness. fill="none" is essential for open traces like polylines, otherwise the browser fills the area between the points with black.

Both accept any CSS color, and because inline SVG shapes are DOM elements, you can move these declarations into a stylesheet (circle { fill: teal; }) or swap them with classes — the standard technique for theme-aware icons. CSS rules override presentation attributes, which makes the attributes good defaults and CSS the customization layer.

The text element places real text at an x,y position — and the y coordinate is the baseline, not the top, which surprises everyone once. Unlike text baked into a PNG, SVG text is selectable, searchable, translatable and readable by assistive technology. Attributes like font-size, font-family and text-anchor (start, middle, end) control its appearance and alignment.
sections.code:
<svg viewBox="0 0 200 60">
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="200" height="60" fill="#eef" stroke="#446" stroke-width="2"></rect>
  <text x="100" y="38" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle" fill="#224">Label</text>
</svg>

sections.heading: Accessibility and the inline vs img decision
sections.body: An SVG that conveys information needs a text alternative. Inline, the tool for that is the title element placed as the first child of the svg: it is never rendered visually, but screen readers announce it and browsers show it as a tooltip. Pair it with role="img" on the svg so assistive technology treats the whole drawing as a single image instead of diving into its shapes. Purely decorative graphics should get aria-hidden="true" instead, so they are skipped entirely. You can also load an SVG file the classic way: . That keeps markup clean, lets the browser cache the file across pages, and the alt attribute handles accessibility. The cost: from HTML you cannot reach inside — no CSS theming of individual shapes, no scripting, and any inside the file replaces nothing about the required alt. The working rule: inline the SVG when you need to style or script its internals (theme-aware icons, interactive charts) or when it is tiny and saving a network request matters; reference it as an image when it is static, reused on many pages, or authored by a design tool and treated as an opaque asset. Either way, sanitize SVG from untrusted sources before inlining — an svg element can legally contain a script element.

lessons.title: Paint pixel graphics from JavaScript with the canvas element
lessons.summary: Use the canvas element and its 2D context to draw rectangles, paths, arcs and text from script — and learn why canvas sizing, fallbacks and accessibility work differently from everything else in HTML.
lessons.goal: Set up a correctly sized canvas with fallback content and a script that draws rectangles, a path with an arc, and text.
lessons.whyItMatters: Canvas is the escape hatch HTML provides when declarative markup is not enough: games, real-time data visualizations, image editors and signature pads all run on it. It behaves unlike any other element — it is a raw bitmap with no DOM inside — so the sizing rules, the accessibility story and the choice between canvas and SVG trip up even experienced developers. Understanding those trade-offs is what separates using canvas from misusing it.
steps: Read the first section to understand what a canvas actually is: a bitmap, not a document.
Study the sizing section carefully — the width/height attribute vs CSS distinction causes most real-world canvas bugs.
In the editor, add the canvas element with proper attributes and fallback text (tasks 1 and 2).
Get the 2d context in the script (task 3).
Draw the filled rectangle, then the path with an arc (tasks 4 and 5).
Add the fillText label, press Run, and confirm every check passes.
lessons.prompt:
<canvas id="scene" width="300" height="150">
  Fallback: a chart of monthly signups would appear here.
</canvas>
<script>
  const ctx = document.getElementById("scene").getContext("2d");
  ctx.fillStyle = "#1565c0";
  ctx.fillRect(10, 10, 120, 60);
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.arc(220, 75, 40, 0, Math.PI * 2);
  ctx.stroke();
  ctx.fillText("Signups 2026", 10, 130);
</script>
lessons.explanation: The width and height attributes give the bitmap 300 by 150 real pixels — sizing with CSS alone would stretch the default bitmap and blur everything. The text between the tags renders only in browsers without canvas support and doubles as a hint for assistive technology. The script asks the element for its 2D drawing context, the object that owns every drawing method: fillRect paints immediately, while arc only defines geometry that the later stroke call inks in. Nothing drawn here exists in the DOM — the result is pure pixels.
lessons.example:
A dashboard needs a live line chart updated 30 times a second with thousands of points. Rendered as SVG, thirty thousand DOM nodes choke the browser.

The same chart on a canvas is one element and one bitmap: each frame the script clears and redraws, and performance stays flat no matter how many points are drawn — the trade being that the chart's contents are invisible to CSS, to right-click-inspect, and to screen readers unless you provide alternatives.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, create a 300 by 150 canvas with meaningful fallback text, then complete the script: get the 2d context, draw a filled and an outlined rectangle, build a path with an arc, and label the drawing with fillText.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a blue filled rectangle, an orange outlined rectangle, a stroked circle, and the label 'Signups 2026' — all painted by script onto one canvas.
commonMistakes: Sizing the canvas with CSS instead of the width/height attributes. CSS scales the default 300x150 bitmap like a stretched image, so drawings come out blurry or distorted.
Forgetting beginPath() before a new shape, so every stroke() re-inks all previously defined path segments and stray lines appear.
Expecting arc() or lineTo() to draw something by themselves — path commands only define geometry; nothing appears until fill() or stroke().
Leaving the fallback area empty. Users of assistive technology get a silent, opaque rectangle; always provide fallback text or an accessible alternative near the canvas.
lessons.proTip: arc() measures angles in radians, not degrees: a full circle is 0 to Math.PI * 2. Keep the conversion factor Math.PI / 180 handy when a design spec gives you degrees.

coding.intro: You will wire up a canvas the professional way — attribute sizing, fallback content — and script a small scene with rectangles, an arc and text.

sections.heading: A bitmap, not a document
sections.body:
The canvas element gives you a rectangular grid of pixels and a JavaScript API to paint them. That is the whole contract. Unlike SVG, where every circle is a DOM node you can select and restyle, a canvas remembers nothing about what you drew — the moment fillRect returns, the browser only knows pixel colors, not 'there is a rectangle here'.

This has direct consequences. You cannot attach a click handler to a shape (only to the whole canvas, doing your own hit-testing math). You cannot restyle a drawn shape with CSS. To change anything you redraw, typically clearing the bitmap and painting the whole frame again. That model is exactly what makes canvas fast: no DOM bookkeeping, just pixels.

In the markup, canvas is deliberately boring: an element with optional width, height and id attributes. All the interesting work happens in script, which is why this lesson's checks look at both your markup and your script source.
sections.code: <canvas id="scene" width="300" height="150"></canvas>

sections.heading: The sizing trap: attributes vs CSS
sections.body:
A canvas has two sizes, and confusing them is the most common canvas bug in production code. The width and height attributes set the bitmap's resolution — how many actual pixels the drawing surface contains. CSS width and height set the display size — how much page area the element occupies. If you set only CSS, the bitmap stays at its default 300 by 150 pixels and the browser stretches it to fit, exactly like scaling up a small photo: everything you draw looks blurry, and coordinates no longer match what the user sees.

The rule: always declare width and height as attributes (or set canvas.width / canvas.height from script, which is the same thing). Use CSS only when you deliberately want scaling, or match the two sizes. On high-density screens, professional code goes one step further: it multiplies the attribute size by window.devicePixelRatio and scales the context, so one CSS pixel maps to several bitmap pixels and lines stay sharp.

One more quirk: assigning to canvas.width or canvas.height at any time wipes the bitmap to transparent black and resets every context setting. It is occasionally used on purpose as a fast clear, and frequently hit by accident in resize handlers.
sections.code:
<!-- Blurry: bitmap is still 300x150, stretched to 600x300 -->
<canvas style="width: 600px; height: 300px"></canvas>

<!-- Sharp: the bitmap really is 600x300 -->
<canvas width="600" height="300"></canvas>

sections.heading: Fallback content and accessibility
sections.body:
Anything you write between <canvas> and </canvas> is fallback content: browsers that support canvas hide it, browsers that do not render it instead. Today every mainstream browser supports canvas, so the fallback's real audience is assistive technology and situations where scripts fail to run.

Because the drawn pixels carry no semantics, a canvas is an accessibility black hole by default: a screen reader finds an element with nothing inside. Mitigations, in increasing order of effort: put a genuine text description in the fallback area; add role="img" with an aria-label summarizing the drawing; render the underlying data as a visually-hidden table or list next to the canvas; or, for interactive canvases, maintain a parallel set of real focusable elements. Never ship the empty tag pair.

Treat the fallback like alt text for a chart: state what the drawing shows and, where possible, the takeaway ('Signups grew from 1,200 to 4,800 during 2026'), not the fact that it is a chart.
sections.code:
<canvas id="chart" width="400" height="200" role="img"
        aria-label="Line chart: signups grew from 1,200 to 4,800 in 2026">
  Signups grew steadily during 2026, from 1,200 in January to 4,800 in December.
</canvas>

sections.heading: Getting a context; rectangles and styles
sections.body:
You never draw on the element directly; you ask it for a drawing context. canvas.getContext("2d") returns a CanvasRenderingContext2D — the object holding every 2D drawing method and all current state. (Other context types exist, like "webgl" for 3D; a canvas can only ever hand out one type.) If you call getContext before the element exists in the DOM, you get null and every later call explodes, so keep the script after the markup or wait for DOMContentLoaded.

The context is a state machine: fillStyle sets the current fill color (any CSS color string, or a gradient/pattern object) and strokeStyle the outline color; lineWidth sets stroke thickness. Those settings stay in force until changed — set fillStyle once and every subsequent fill uses it.

Rectangles are the only shape with dedicated one-call methods: fillRect(x, y, w, h) paints a solid rectangle immediately, strokeRect draws just the outline, and clearRect erases a region to transparency — the standard way to wipe a frame before redrawing.

sections.heading: Paths, arcs and text
sections.body:
Every non-rectangle shape is built as a path: a list of geometry commands that draw nothing by themselves. beginPath() starts a fresh list — skip it and new segments pile onto the old ones, a classic source of mystery lines. moveTo(x, y) lifts the pen to a start point; lineTo(x, y) adds a straight segment; arc(cx, cy, radius, startAngle, endAngle) adds a circular arc around a center point, with angles in radians measured clockwise from the positive x-axis. A full circle is arc(cx, cy, r, 0, Math.PI * 2). closePath() optionally joins the last point back to the first.

Once the geometry is defined, fill() paints its interior with the current fillStyle and stroke() inks its outline with the current strokeStyle. You can call both on the same path for a filled, outlined shape.

Text works without paths: fillText("label", x, y) paints text at a baseline position using the context's font property (same syntax as CSS font, e.g. "16px sans-serif"); strokeText draws outlined letters and measureText reports how wide a string will render — essential for centering. Canvas text is pixels like everything else: not selectable, not translatable, not read by screen readers, so any essential wording must also exist as real HTML.

sections.heading: Canvas or SVG? The decision rule
sections.body:
Both technologies draw graphics; they occupy opposite ends of one trade-off. SVG is retained-mode: the browser keeps every shape as a DOM node, so you get CSS styling, per-shape events, easy accessibility and crisp scaling for free — but each node costs memory and layout work, and tens of thousands of them become slow. Canvas is immediate-mode: you get one dumb bitmap that renders anything at high speed, and you personally take over everything the DOM would have done — hit-testing, redrawing, accessibility, resolution handling.

The working rule: choose SVG when the graphic has a modest number of meaningful shapes (icons, logos, diagrams, ordinary charts) and canvas when you have very many objects or high-frequency redraws (games, particle effects, 60fps streaming visualizations, pixel-level image manipulation). If you find yourself writing hit-testing math for a static diagram, you picked canvas too early; if your SVG chart stutters while animating thousands of points, it is time to switch.

On this platform the checks parse your code without executing it, so the canvas tasks verify two things: the markup (element, sizing attributes, fallback) via the document, and the drawing calls via patterns in your script source.

lessons.title: Stamp out repeating markup with template, slot and web components
lessons.summary: Use the template element as an inert blueprint you clone from script, understand slots and shadow DOM conceptually, and know when custom elements are worth their weight.
lessons.goal: Build a card blueprint inside a template — including a named slot — and clone it into the page from script.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every application renders repeating structures: product cards, table rows, notifications. Duplicating that markup by string-concatenation in JavaScript is fragile and invites injection bugs; the template element keeps the blueprint as real, parser-checked HTML that scripts stamp out on demand. Templates, slots, shadow DOM and custom elements together form the web components standard — the browser-native answer to reusable UI, and the foundation of many design systems you will integrate with even if you never author one.
steps: Read how template content is parsed but inert — the key property everything else builds on.
In the editor, create the card template with its internal structure (tasks 1 and 2).
Add the named slot placeholder inside the blueprint (task 3).
Read the cloning section, then clone the template's content in the script (task 4).
Fill the clone and append it to the cards container (task 5).
Skim the shadow DOM and custom elements sections — you need the concepts more than the code today.
lessons.explanation: The template holds a fully parsed card that the browser never renders, loads no resources for, and keeps out of document.querySelector's reach — an inert blueprint. tpl.content exposes that blueprint as a DocumentFragment; cloneNode(true) copies the entire subtree so the original stays pristine for the next card. The script fills the copy's fields safely via textContent and appends it, at which point — and only then — the markup goes live. The named slot marks where a component user could inject their own avatar markup once this blueprint is used inside a shadow root.
lessons.example:
A team page builds twelve member cards by gluing HTML strings together in JavaScript: quotes get mismatched, a member name containing an ampersand breaks the layout, and the markup exists nowhere the HTML validator can see.

Moved into a template element, the card markup is written once as real HTML, validated with the rest of the page, and the script shrinks to: clone, fill two fields with textContent, append. Adding a thirteenth card is a data change, not a markup change.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, build the card blueprint inside a template element — heading, paragraph, and a named slot — then complete the script that clones the blueprint, fills in the member's name, and appends the card to the page.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows the page heading plus one rendered card reading 'Ada Lovelace — Engineer', stamped from the template; the template itself stays invisible.
commonMistakes: Appending tpl.content directly instead of a clone. A fragment's nodes MOVE when inserted, so the template is emptied and the second stamp produces nothing.
Calling cloneNode() without true. The default is a shallow copy — you get an empty fragment with none of the card's children.
Trying to reach template contents with document.querySelector. Template content lives in a separate inert fragment; query tpl.content instead.
Reaching for a full custom element (or a framework) when one template plus ten lines of script would do — web components earn their complexity only when reuse crosses page or team boundaries.
lessons.proTip: Fill cloned templates with element.textContent, never innerHTML. textContent treats data as text no matter what it contains, which closes off HTML-injection bugs by construction.

coding.intro: You will write a card blueprint that the browser parses but never renders, then stamp a live copy of it into the page from script.

sections.heading: template: parsed but inert
sections.body:
The template element is a holding pen for markup. Everything inside it is parsed like normal HTML — typos are corrected, the tree is built — but the result is deliberately inert: it does not render, images and videos inside it do not load, scripts inside it do not run, and form controls inside it are ignored by the surrounding form. It is markup on standby.

The inertness is the feature. Before template existed, developers hid blueprint markup in display:none divs (resources still loaded, ids collided, screen readers sometimes found it) or embedded HTML strings in JavaScript (no validation, injection-prone). A template gives you a place to keep repeating structures as genuine HTML with none of those costs.

One consequence surprises everyone: document.querySelector cannot see inside a template. The children are not document nodes — they live in a private DocumentFragment attached to the element. Even this platform's selector checks cannot look in there, which is why the tasks below verify your template's internals against the raw source instead.

sections.heading: content and cloneNode: stamping copies
sections.body:
The blueprint is exposed to script as templateElement.content — a DocumentFragment holding the parsed children. A fragment is a lightweight container: when you insert it into the document, the fragment itself vanishes and its children move in its place.

That moving behavior is why you clone. If you append tpl.content directly, the children relocate into the page and the template is left empty — the second card you try to stamp comes out blank. The correct pattern is tpl.content.cloneNode(true): a deep copy (true means 'include all descendants'; the default false copies only the empty fragment) that you fill in and insert while the original stays untouched.

Fill the clone before or after inserting — before is tidier — using clone.querySelector to find the fields and textContent to set them. querySelector works fine on the fragment; it is only the document-level lookup that cannot see template internals. Finally, appendChild (or append) on some container element makes the copy live: this is the moment the markup starts rendering and behaving like normal DOM.

sections.heading: slot: leaving holes on purpose
sections.body: A template with fixed fields covers repetition, but reusable components need flexibility: 'here is a card — put whatever you like in the avatar corner'. The slot element exists for exactly that. Inside a component's internal markup, marks an insertion point; when the component is used, the user's own child elements are projected into that hole at render time. A bare is the default slot: it receives all of the user's children that are not claimed elsewhere. A named slot — — receives only elements that opt in with a matching slot attribute, like . One component can offer several named holes plus a default one, and anything you write between the slot's own tags serves as fallback content shown when the user supplies nothing. Slots only actually project content when the internal markup lives in a shadow root (next section); written in a plain template they are simply part of the blueprint, waiting. The mental model to keep: template answers 'what does the component look like inside?', slot answers 'where does the user's content go?'.
sections.code: Loves analytical engines.

sections.heading: Shadow DOM in one section
sections.body:
Shadow DOM gives an element a private, encapsulated subtree. element.attachShadow({ mode: "open" }) creates a shadow root; whatever you place inside it renders in the element's place, but the outside page's CSS selectors do not reach in, the component's internal styles do not leak out, and document.querySelector does not see the internals. It is a boundary — the reason a third-party date-picker cannot be shattered by your site's aggressive * { margin: 0 } rule, and vice versa.

The three technologies interlock: a component clones a template, appends the clone into its shadow root, and the slots inside that shadow tree pull the user's light-DOM children into position. Browsers themselves use shadow DOM internally — the play controls of a video element are a shadow tree you can reveal in DevTools by enabling 'show user agent shadow DOM'.

Encapsulation cuts both ways: global theming, form participation and some accessibility relationships get harder across the boundary. Treat shadow DOM as a tool for hard isolation, not a default for every widget.

sections.heading: Custom elements: awareness level
sections.body:
The last piece of the standard lets you register your own tags. customElements.define("team-card", TeamCard) associates a tag name with a class extending HTMLElement; from then on every <team-card> in markup upgrades into an instance of that class. Custom tag names must contain a hyphen — that is how the parser distinguishes them from possible future built-ins.

The class receives lifecycle callbacks: connectedCallback runs when the element enters the document (the usual place to attach a shadow root and stamp the template), disconnectedCallback when it leaves, and attributeChangedCallback when one of the attributes listed in a static observedAttributes array changes. Together with template, slot and shadow DOM, this is a complete component model with zero dependencies.

You do not need to author custom elements to work professionally, but you must recognize the pattern: design systems (used across Google, Adobe, and many enterprises) ship as custom elements precisely because they work identically in React, Vue and plain HTML.

sections.heading: Where components shine — and where they are overkill
sections.body:
Web components earn their keep when UI must be reused across page, project or framework boundaries: a design system consumed by three teams on three stacks, an embeddable widget dropped into arbitrary customer sites, or a leaf component (icon button, tag chip, rating stars) whose styling must survive any host page. The browser-native contract — just HTML tags — is the most durable interface the platform offers.

They are overkill for markup repeated within a single page or app: a template plus a few lines of cloning script (exactly what you build in this lesson) solves that with a fraction of the concepts. They also duplicate machinery you already have if your project runs on a component framework — React or Vue components fill the same role internally, and mixing the two models adds friction around events, forms and server-side rendering.

A pragmatic ladder: start with a template and a loop; reach for a custom element when the same UI must cross a boundary; add shadow DOM only when you need real style isolation, not just tidiness.

sections.heading: Dragging is opt-in: the draggable attribute
sections.body:
HTML ships a complete drag-and-drop system, but almost nothing participates by default: only links, images and text selections are natively draggable. Any other element joins by declaring draggable="true". The value is an enumerated string, not a boolean attribute — draggable alone or draggable="" does not work reliably, so always write the explicit ="true".

Once an element is draggable, the browser handles the physics: the ghost image following the cursor, the forbidden-cursor over invalid targets, the cross-window and even cross-application drag (dragging text into another program). Your JavaScript's job is only to answer two questions: what data does this drag carry, and which targets accept it.

Accessibility note: drag-and-drop is mouse-and-touch-centric. Professional implementations keep a keyboard path to the same outcome — a 'move to' button or menu — because the native API offers no built-in keyboard interaction.

sections.heading: The event chain and dataTransfer
sections.body:
A drag fires a fixed sequence of events. On the dragged element: dragstart when the drag begins, drag repeatedly while moving, dragend when it finishes. On whatever the cursor passes over: dragenter, dragover (fired continuously, many times per second), dragleave, and finally drop on the target that accepts.

The two sides of a drag never share variables directly — the drop target might be in another window entirely. The bridge is the event's dataTransfer object: in dragstart you call e.dataTransfer.setData(type, value), and in drop you read it back with getData(type). The type is a MIME-style label; "text/plain" is the workhorse. Values are strings only — the standard pattern for moving DOM elements is to store the element's id and re-find it on drop.

For security, the data is readable only in the drop handler — during dragover you can see the types on offer but not the values, so a page you merely drag across cannot steal the payload.

sections.heading: The one line everyone forgets: preventDefault on dragover
sections.body:
Here is the design decision that generates a thousand bug reports: by default, every element REJECTS drops. The browser's default action for dragover is 'this is not a valid drop target'. To accept drops, a target must cancel that default by calling e.preventDefault() inside its dragover (and ideally dragenter) handler. Do nothing, and your drop handler simply never fires — no error, no warning, nothing.

Once dragover is cancelled, the drop event can fire. In the drop handler you call preventDefault() again (otherwise some browsers perform their own default, like navigating to a dropped link), read the payload with getData, and act — here, appendChild moves the dragged element into the zone. appendChild on an element already in the document relocates it; no cloning or deleting needed.

The dataTransfer.dropEffect property ("move", "copy", "link") set during dragover controls which cursor the OS shows, a small touch that makes the interaction feel native.

sections.heading: Geolocation: asking where the user is
sections.body:
The Geolocation API lives at navigator.geolocation and answers one question: where is this device? Its main method, getCurrentPosition(successCallback, errorCallback, options), is fully asynchronous — the browser may consult GPS, Wi-Fi networks or IP databases, and above all it must first ask the user. A permission prompt appears on first use, and your code has no say in the answer.

On success, your first callback receives a position object. position.coords carries the useful fields: latitude and longitude in decimal degrees, accuracy as a radius in meters, and — when the hardware provides them — altitude, heading and speed, which are null otherwise. position.timestamp records when the fix was taken.

An optional third argument tunes the request: { enableHighAccuracy: true } requests GPS-grade fixes (slower, battery-hungry), timeout caps the wait in milliseconds, and maximumAge allows a cached fix. For live tracking there is watchPosition, which invokes your callback on every movement and returns an id for clearWatch — always clear it, or you drain the battery of every user who leaves the map open.

sections.heading: Failure is normal: errors, permissions, HTTPS
sections.body:
Treat the error callback as a first-class code path, not an afterthought. Its error argument has a code with three values: 1 PERMISSION_DENIED (the user said no, or policy blocks it), 2 POSITION_UNAVAILABLE (no signal — underground, hardware off), 3 TIMEOUT (your timeout elapsed first). Each deserves a different reaction: denial should switch to manual input without nagging, unavailability might suggest retrying, timeout might retry with lower accuracy.

Geolocation is restricted to secure contexts: pages served over HTTPS (localhost counts as secure for development). On plain HTTP the API is simply absent or rejects immediately — a classic 'works on my machine, dies in production' trap when production forgets a redirect to HTTPS.

Design etiquette: request location on a user gesture (a 'Use my location' button), never on page load — an unexplained permission prompt is the fastest way to a permanent denial, and browsers remember the answer. And since users can revoke permission at any time, every release must keep the no-location path working.

lessons.whyItMatters: These three APIs answer questions every real application eventually asks. Where do I keep the user's settings between visits without a server round-trip? Web storage. Why does the page freeze while I crunch this dataset? Move it to a worker. How do users see new data without hammering refresh? Server-Sent Events. Knowing the boundaries — strings only, no DOM in workers, one-way SSE — is what lets you pick the right tool instead of fighting the wrong one.

The EventSource opens a long-lived HTTP connection that the server pushes messages down; the browser parses each one into an onmessage event and reconnects by itself if the line drops.

sections.heading: Two storages, one API
sections.body:
The browser gives every origin two key-value stores with an identical API and one crucial difference: lifetime. localStorage persists until explicitly deleted — close the tab, reboot the machine, the data is still there. sessionStorage lives and dies with the tab: each tab gets its own copy, and closing the tab wipes it. Same site open in two tabs means one shared localStorage but two independent sessionStorages.

The API is four methods and a property: setItem(key, value) writes, getItem(key) reads (returning null — not undefined, not an error — when the key is absent), removeItem(key) deletes one entry, clear() deletes everything for the origin, and length reports the entry count. All operations are synchronous, which keeps the code simple but means giant values can briefly stall the page.

Scope and limits: storage is partitioned by origin — scheme plus host plus port — so https://app.example.com cannot read another origin's data, and nothing you store is ever sent to any server automatically. Budget is roughly 5 MB per origin per store; exceeding it throws a QuotaExceededError, so wrap large writes in try/catch. Users can wipe storage at any time, and private-browsing modes may discard it aggressively: treat it as a convenience cache, never as the only copy of anything important.

sections.heading: Strings only: the JSON round-trip
sections.body:
Both stores hold strings and nothing else. Store a number and you get a string back; store an object and JavaScript helpfully converts it to "[object Object]", destroying the data. The universal idiom is the JSON round-trip: JSON.stringify(value) on the way in, JSON.parse(text) on the way out. It handles objects, arrays, numbers, booleans and nesting — everything JSON can express (functions and Dates need special handling; Dates come back as strings).

Read defensively: the key may not exist yet (first visit), and getItem then returns null. The compact guard is JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("prefs")) followed by a null check, or a default via || / ?? on the parsed result. A corrupted value makes JSON.parse throw, so production code often wraps the read in try/catch and falls back to defaults.

Where do cookies fit? Cookies are the older mechanism with one defining behavior storage lacks: they are attached to every HTTP request to the server, which makes them the right home for session identifiers the server must see — and the wrong home for anything bulky, since they are capped near 4 KB and inflate every request. The modern division of labor: cookies for server-facing session state, web storage for client-only data like preferences, drafts and caches.

sections.heading: Web Workers: a second thread
sections.body:
JavaScript in a page runs on one thread — the same thread that paints pixels and reacts to clicks. Run a heavy computation there and the whole interface freezes: no scrolling, no typing, eventually a 'page unresponsive' warning. A dedicated Web Worker escapes this by running a separate script file on a separate thread: new Worker("stats-worker.js") starts it, and it computes in parallel while the page stays fluid.

The isolation is strict. A worker has no DOM: no document, no window, no access to the page's variables — attempts throw immediately. It gets its own global scope (self) with the essentials: fetch, timers, and importScripts for loading libraries. This is by design: two threads mutating one DOM would need locks and all the bugs that come with them, so the platform simply forbids sharing.

All communication is message passing. Either side calls postMessage(data) and the other receives it in an onmessage handler as e.data; the data is structured-cloned — copied, not shared, so there is no aliasing to reason about. When the worker is done for good, terminate() from the page (or self.close() inside) frees the thread. Reach for a worker whenever a computation would block the page noticeably — parsing large files, crunching numbers, image processing; skip it for quick work, since spawning threads and copying messages has its own cost.

sections.heading: Server-Sent Events: the server pushes
sections.body:
Ordinary HTTP is client-initiated: nothing arrives unless the page asks. When the server has news — a fresh notification, a price change, a build finishing — the crude answer is polling on a timer, which is both laggy and wasteful. Server-Sent Events invert the flow: the page opens one long-lived HTTP connection with new EventSource(url), and the server keeps it open, writing a message down the pipe whenever it likes.

The browser side is almost no code. Each server message fires the EventSource's onmessage handler with the payload in e.data (always text; send JSON and parse it). Servers can label messages with custom event names, which you receive via addEventListener("price", ...) instead of onmessage. The killer feature is built-in resilience: if the connection drops, the browser reconnects automatically, and a Last-Event-ID header lets the server resume where the stream broke — logic you would have to hand-write with anything else.

On the wire it is disarmingly simple: a text/event-stream response where each message is a line like data: hello followed by a blank line. Any web framework can produce it; no special server or protocol upgrade needed.

sections.heading: SSE or WebSocket? And what runs where
sections.body:
SSE is one-way: server to client, over plain HTTP. WebSocket is two-way: after an HTTP handshake it upgrades to its own protocol, and both sides can send at any time. That single difference decides the choice. Notifications, live scores, progress feeds, dashboards — the client only listens, so SSE wins on simplicity: normal HTTP infrastructure, automatic reconnection, a ten-line client. Chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing — the client talks constantly, so WebSocket is the right tool despite its heavier operational footprint. (The client can still 'talk' in an SSE architecture — it just uses ordinary fetch requests alongside the stream.)

A note about this lesson's editor: checks parse your code without executing it, and the sandbox has no worker file to load and no SSE endpoint to stream from. That is why the worker and feed code live inside named functions the page defines but does not call — the pattern is real and portable, and the checks verify it in your source.

lessons.whyItMatters: Browsers forgive almost anything, so bad HTML 'works' — right up until a teammate has to edit it, a validator has to check it, or a parser edge case bites in production. Style conventions exist because code is read far more than written: consistent, lowercase, quoted, fully-closed markup diffs cleanly in code review, survives copy-paste between projects, and never depends on parser guesswork. Recognizing deprecated elements matters too: you will inherit old codebases, and knowing the modern replacement for each relic is routine maintenance work.

lessons.example:
A freelancer inherits a 2009-era portfolio page: uppercase tags, unquoted attributes, a <center><font size=5> heading, no doctype, no charset. It renders — browsers heroically guess — but the client's new CMS mangles the unquoted attributes, accented characters display as garbage on one host, and the validator emits a wall of errors.

After the cleanup pass, the page is boring in the best way: standard skeleton, one h1, styling hooks via classes for CSS, alt text on the image. The validator is silent and any developer can extend the page without archaeology.

sections.heading: Why conventions exist when browsers do not care
sections.body:
HTML is unusual among languages: almost nothing is enforced. Uppercase tags parse, unquoted attributes parse, unclosed elements parse. So style rules are not about pleasing the browser — they are about the humans and tools downstream. A teammate scanning a diff, a validator checking correctness, a templating engine embedding your markup, a designer copying a snippet: all of them benefit when the code has one predictable shape.

The professional baseline, in one paragraph: lowercase element and attribute names; every attribute value in double quotes; every element you open, you close — including the ones where closing is technically optional; consistent indentation (two spaces is the common default) with nesting always reflected; and lines kept to a sane length so side-by-side diffs stay readable.

Lowercase won for concrete reasons: it is easier to type, visually calmer next to mixed-case content, and mandatory anyway in XML-based contexts, so the habit travels. Quoting won because unquoted values are a time bomb — class=my box silently becomes class="my" plus a stray attribute box, and the layout bug appears in a different file from the typo.

sections.heading: The non-negotiables of every document
sections.body:
Five things appear in every page a professional ships, without discussion. <!DOCTYPE html> on line one — omit it and browsers drop into quirks mode, emulating 1990s bugs, which changes how CSS box sizing behaves. lang on the html element (lang="en") — screen readers pick pronunciation rules from it, translation tools use it, and search engines read it. <meta charset="UTF-8"> as the first thing in head — declared late or never, and any non-ASCII character can render as mojibake on servers that do not send the encoding header.

Completing the set: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">, without which phones render a zoomed-out desktop layout; and a unique, descriptive <title>, which becomes the tab label, the bookmark name and the search-result headline. To these, accessibility adds a sixth that is just as non-negotiable: every img carries alt — descriptive text for informative images, alt="" for purely decorative ones so screen readers skip them.

None of these five produce visible errors when missing. That is exactly why they belong to a checklist: the failure modes (quirks mode, garbled text, unpinchable mobile pages, untitled tabs) surface later, elsewhere, to someone else.

</head>

sections.heading: Structure discipline: closing, nesting, indenting
sections.body:
HTML lets you skip some closing tags: ,

, and a few others are optional per the spec, and , , can even be omitted entirely. Professional style ignores those permissions. Explicit closing makes nesting visible, prevents the parser's auto-closing rules from producing a tree you did not intend (a

containing a list silently closes before the list — the parser decides, not you), and keeps markup portable into stricter contexts like XML feeds and some templating systems. Indentation mirrors the tree: children one level deeper than parents, siblings aligned. Two spaces per level is the widespread convention — deep enough to see structure, shallow enough that realistic nesting fits on screen. Do not indent with tabs and spaces mixed; pick one (the project's formatter decides) and let it be boring. Void elements — img, br, meta, input, hr, link — have no content and take no closing tag. Writing them with a trailing slash (
) is harmless in HTML and required in XHTML; modern HTML style omits the slash. Just be consistent with whatever the codebase already does.

sections.heading: Names, classes, and keeping style out of markup
sections.body:
Class names are the vocabulary your HTML shares with CSS and JavaScript, so name them by role, not appearance: price-total, nav-primary, card-featured — not red-text, big-box, left-div. Appearance changes (the 'red' text becomes orange in the rebrand) should never force an HTML edit. Pick one casing convention — kebab-case is the CSS-world default — and never mix camelCase, snake_case and kebab-case in one project.

Inline styles (style="color: red") are the corresponding anti-pattern: they scatter presentation across the markup, win specificity fights against your stylesheet in confusing ways, and cannot be reused, cached or themed. Legitimate exceptions are narrow: values computed at runtime by scripts, and HTML email, where stylesheets are poorly supported. Everything else belongs in a stylesheet reached via class.

Two small hygiene rules complete the picture: keep attribute order roughly consistent (a common order is class, id, name, data-*, src/href, everything else, aria-*) so eyes can scan tags quickly, and avoid redundant attributes the spec defaults anyway (type="text/css" on link, type="text/javascript" on script).

sections.heading: HTML vs XHTML: why the strict dialect matters historically
sections.body:
XHTML was the early-2000s attempt to rebuild HTML on XML rules: every tag lowercase, every attribute quoted, every element closed (void elements as
), one single root element, and — crucially — draconian error handling. Serve real XHTML and one unescaped ampersand replaces your page with a parser error screen. The web chose forgiveness instead: HTML5 defined precisely how browsers recover from every possible malformation, and XHTML's strictness survives mainly in XML-based systems (RSS/Atom feeds, EPUB, some CMS pipelines) and in inline SVG, which follows XML rules for things like attribute casing. The useful takeaway is not the history but the habit: professional HTML style is essentially 'write as strictly as XHTML demanded, inside a parser that forgives you'. Code written that way is simultaneously valid HTML5 and trivially convertible to any XML context — you get the robustness without the error screens. You will still meet the XHTML doctype and xmlns attributes in older codebases. Recognize them, do not imitate them: new documents get and nothing more.

<html lang="en">

sections.heading: The deprecated blacklist and its replacements
sections.body:
HTML's early years produced presentational elements that later versions removed; browsers still render most of them for backward compatibility, which is exactly why you must recognize them on sight — they will not error, they will just quietly mark a codebase as unmaintained. The blacklist: <font> (use CSS font properties via a class), <center> (CSS text-align or margin auto), <big> and <small>-as-styling (CSS font-size), <strike> and <s>-as-styling (CSS text-decoration, or <del> when the meaning is 'removed content'), <u>-as-styling (CSS again), <marquee> and <blink> (CSS animations, used with restraint), <tt> (CSS monospace font or <code> when it really is code).

Gone with more force: the frame family — <frameset>, <frame>, <noframes> — which HTML5 removed outright; layouts that once used frames are built with CSS, and embedding another page is <iframe>'s job. Also retired: <acronym> (use <abbr>), <basefont>, <applet>, and the presentational attributes that infested markup — align, bgcolor, border on non-tables, valign — all replaced by CSS properties.

The pattern behind every replacement is the same separation of concerns you have practiced all course: HTML says what content is, CSS says how it looks. When you meet a deprecated element in the wild, the refactor is mechanical: find the visual intent, express it in a class, delete the relic.

lessons.whyItMatters: HTML never crashes, and that is precisely the danger: a broken page renders anyway, differently repaired by different parsers, and the bug surfaces as a mysterious CSS or JavaScript failure weeks later. Professionals do not debug HTML by staring at the rendered page — they compare the source against the DOM the parser actually built, and they let the validator find what eyes miss. This workflow turns hour-long mystery hunts into two-minute fixes.

sections.heading: Browsers never throw — they guess
sections.body:
Most languages stop at the first syntax error. HTML does the opposite: the HTML5 specification defines, for every possible malformation, exactly how a browser must repair it and keep going. Unclosed tag? Close it at a spec-defined point. Element somewhere illegal? Relocate it. Impossible nesting? Rearrange it. The upside is a web where twenty-five years of imperfect pages still render. The downside lands on you: your mistakes are hidden, not reported. The danger is that repair is a guess about your intent, and the guess becomes the real page. CSS selectors match against the repaired tree, not your source. JavaScript queries the repaired tree. So an HTML mistake almost never looks like an HTML mistake — it surfaces as 'my selector doesn't match' or 'the element is not where I put it', two files away from the typo that caused it. Classic repairs to know by sight: an open

auto-closes when a block element arrives (so a list 'inside' a paragraph actually ends it); a written without gets one inserted, breaking naive table > tr selectors; content placed illegally between table cells is hoisted out above the table entirely; and a stray closing tag with no open partner is simply deleted.

sections.heading: Two views of the truth: view-source vs the Elements panel
sections.body:
Every browser offers two very different ways to look at a page, and debugging HTML is largely the art of comparing them. View-source (Ctrl+U / Cmd+Option+U) shows the raw bytes the server sent — your file, untouched. The DevTools Elements panel (right-click, Inspect) shows the live DOM: the tree after parser repairs, and after any JavaScript modifications. When the two disagree, the difference IS the bug report.

A practical diffing routine: pick the element that misbehaves, find it in view-source, then find it in the Elements panel and compare its parent chain. Is it inside the parent you wrote? Did it gain or lose siblings? Did an element you opened get closed earlier than you intended? Parser adoptions — an element sitting in a different parent than in your source — are the smoking gun of a markup error somewhere above it.

The Elements panel earns its place beyond diffing: hover to highlight the element on the page, see which elements exist but have zero size, and use the search (Ctrl+F inside the panel) with a CSS selector to check what your stylesheet's selector actually matches. Remember its one trap: it always looks valid, because the parser has already cleaned up — absence of red flags there is not absence of errors.

sections.heading: The W3C validator workflow
sections.body:
The Nu HTML Checker at validator.w3.org is the authoritative second opinion: it parses your page with the same rules browsers use, but reports every repair instead of hiding it. It accepts a URL, an uploaded file, or pasted source — the paste mode fits an edit-validate loop best. Output is a list of messages, each with a severity, an explanation, and the line and column where the parser noticed the problem.

Read messages with two rules in mind. First, the reported line is where the parser NOTICED, not necessarily where you erred — an unclosed <div> on line 12 is often reported as 'unexpected end of file' at the bottom. Second, severities differ: errors are genuine violations; warnings flag legal-but-suspect patterns (a section without a heading, an obsolete attribute). Fix errors always; read warnings and decide.

The workflow that keeps you sane: validate, fix ONLY the first error or two, re-validate. Early errors cascade — one unclosed quote can generate fifty phantom messages — so a 50-error report frequently collapses to three real problems after the first fix. Working bottom-up, by contrast, means fixing phantoms.

Error: Duplicate ID 'intro'.
  -> two elements share an id; anchors and getElementById use the first

Error: An 'img' element must have an 'alt' attribute.
  -> add a description, or alt="" if decorative

sections.heading: The greatest hits: common errors and their fixes
sections.body: A handful of messages account for most validation reports. 'Missing doctype' — add as line one; without it the page renders in quirks mode with legacy box-model behavior. 'Element head is missing a required instance of child element title' — every document needs a non-empty . 'An img element must have an alt attribute' — describe the image, or explicitly opt out with alt="" for decoration. 'Duplicate ID' — ids must be unique per page; rename one and update whatever referenced it. 'Stray end tag' — you closed something never opened, usually the residue of a half-finished edit; delete it. Nesting errors form the second family: 'Element X not allowed as child of element Y'. The frequent offenders: li outside ul/ol, block elements inside <p>, <a> wrapped around another <a>, form controls outside any form when their attributes assume one. The fix is always structural — give the element its legal parent — never cosmetic. Attribute errors round it out: unquoted values containing spaces, obsolete presentational attributes (align, bgcolor), and misspelled attribute names, which HTML silently treats as unknown-but-legal, making the validator the only tool that will ever tell you about a mistyped 'herf'.

sections.heading: This platform's console is a mini-validator
sections.body:
The feedback console under the editor works on the validator's principle, scaled to each lesson: it parses your code the way a browser would (using the same DOM parsing machinery, with no JavaScript execution) and then runs the lesson's checks against the parsed result. A failing check is a validator message with a friendlier voice — it names the missing or malformed piece and, like the validator, judges the parsed tree rather than your raw text.

That detail explains behavior you may have noticed across this course: writing an element inside a template, or markup so broken the parser relocated it, can fail a selector check even though the text is 'right there' in your editor. The check queries the DOM the parser built — exactly as your CSS and JavaScript would in production. When a check fails unexpectedly, apply this lesson's routine: assume a parser repair, and look above the reported element for the unclosed or misplaced tag that triggered it.

Carry the habit outward: editor and console here, DevTools plus the W3C validator everywhere else. The loop is identical — parse, read the first complaint, fix, re-run — and it is the difference between debugging by evidence and debugging by superstition.

Nobody experienced writes a page top-to-bottom in one go. The professional sequence starts before any tags: a content inventory — listing what the page must contain (for Brewmate: hero image, feature claims, comparison data, a demo video, an email signup, FAQ answers, company details) and what each piece IS (tabular data? a media object? a form?). The inventory decides the elements; design decides only how they will look, later, in CSS.

Then the passes. Pass one builds the semantic skeleton: landmarks, headings, empty sections — and verifies it while the page is still ten lines long, because a structural mistake found now costs nothing. Pass two drops media into the standing frame. Pass three builds forms and interactive pieces. Pass four fills the head with metadata. The final pass validates and reads the whole document as an outline.

This order is not ceremony; it front-loads the decisions that are expensive to reverse. Moving a video element is trivial; discovering after four hundred lines that your 'sections' should have been articles inside one section is an afternoon of re-nesting.

sections.heading: Pass 1 — the semantic skeleton and the skip link
sections.body:
The frame uses one of each landmark: header for the site identity and navigation, nav (with aria-label when a page has several) for the link group, main — exactly one per page — for the unique content, footer for the address and small print. Inside main, each distinct topic gets a section with its own heading and id; self-contained pieces that would make sense syndicated elsewhere (a feature story, a testimonial) get article. Screen-reader users receive this structure as a navigable map: landmark-jumping is to them what visual scanning is to everyone else.

The first focusable element on the page is the skip link: <a href="#main"> pointing at main's id. Keyboard users otherwise tab through every navigation link on every page before reaching content; one link erases that toll. It is usually styled off-screen until focused — but the styling is CSS's problem; the HTML contract is just the link and its target.

The nav links each carry a data-section attribute naming their target. The data-* mechanism is HTML's sanctioned way to attach machine-readable metadata: scripts read it via element.dataset.section to highlight the active link on scroll, with no classes abused as data storage and no href parsing.

The hero image ships in two sizes because one file cannot serve both a phone and a desktop monitor efficiently. The picture element handles the art direction: source elements with media conditions are evaluated top to bottom, the first match wins, and the img child is both the fallback and the carrier of alt text — a picture without a proper img inside renders nothing. For pure resolution switching without art direction, srcset with width descriptors directly on the img would do the same job with less markup.

The demo video uses the video element with controls (never autoplay a product page with sound), width to reserve layout space, and poster — the preview frame shown before play, which otherwise defaults to a black rectangle or an arbitrary first frame. Inside, source elements offer formats and the text fallback covers ancient browsers and, more realistically, gives crawlers and copy-pasted contexts something to say.

Had the brief called for an external player instead, the iframe route has its own two rules: a title attribute describing the embed (screen readers announce iframes by title, and 'iframe' alone is useless) and loading="lazy" so below-the-fold embeds do not tax initial page load.

sections.heading: Pass 3 — the comparison table and the contact form
sections.body:
The model-comparison data is genuinely tabular — two models rated against the same features — so it gets a real table, never a grid of divs. The professional minimum: a caption naming the table (announced first by screen readers, useful to everyone scanning), th cells with scope="col" for the model columns and scope="row" for feature rows, so a reader navigating cell by cell always hears which feature and which model a value belongs to.

The signup form is where accessibility and validation meet. Every control pairs with a label via for/id — clicking the label focuses the field, and screen readers announce the field's purpose. Related controls group inside a fieldset with a legend ('Contact details'), which is announced as context for every field within. Validation is declarative: type="email" makes the browser check the format, required blocks empty submission, and the browser's built-in messages localize for free. Server-side validation still exists — client validation is user convenience, not security.

The FAQ uses details/summary: native disclosure widgets with keyboard support and no JavaScript. The footer carries address — the element is specifically for contact information of the page's owner — and the launch date in a time element with a machine-readable datetime attribute, so calendars and crawlers can parse what humans read as prose.

sections.heading: Pass 4 — metadata: what search and social actually read
sections.body:
The head already carries the course's non-negotiables (charset, viewport, title). The capstone adds the discovery layer. <meta name="description"> supplies the sentence search engines usually show under your title — around 150 characters, written like ad copy for the click, unique per page.

Open Graph tags control the card that appears when the page is shared in chat apps and social feeds: og:title, og:description, and og:image name the headline, blurb and picture of that card. Note the attribute: Open Graph uses property="og:...", not name — a mixup here fails silently, the single most common metadata bug. Without these tags, sharers get a bare URL or a scraped guess; with them, every share is a designed preview.

The title itself deserves one last look: it should read distinctly in a row of pinned tabs and in a search result — 'Brewmate — smart coffee scale' beats both 'Home' and a keyword pile. Title, description and og tags routinely repeat similar text; that is normal, they serve three different consumers.
sections.code:
<meta name="description" content="Brewmate, the smart coffee scale for home baristas.">
<meta property="og:title" content="Brewmate smart coffee scale">
<meta property="og:description" content="Dial in every cup with live brew tracking.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://brewmate.example/card.jpg">

sections.heading: The final pass: verification as a habit
sections.body:
A professional page ends with a verification ritual, and the capstone is the place to make it muscle memory. Read the headings alone: do h1 'Brewmate' and the section h2s form a sensible table of contents with no skipped levels? Walk the landmarks: exactly one main, header and footer at top level, every section titled. Tab through the page: does focus land on the skip link first, then move through nav, form and button in reading order?

Then the mechanical checks, exactly as the previous lesson practiced: every img has alt, every form control a label, every iframe (if any) a title, ids unique, required head elements present. Run the document through the validator — or here, the feedback console — and clear findings top-down.

What you have at the end is more than an exercise: it is a complete, valid, semantic, accessible page skeleton with media, forms, and metadata — the 20 percent of HTML that carries 95 percent of every real project. Styling it is CSS's story; behavior is JavaScript's. The structure, from here on, is yours.
